quiz.q: How fast does insertion sort run when the array is already sorted?
options: It runs in O(n) linear time because each element is checked once.
It takes O(n²) time because all pairs must still be swapped.
It degrades to O(n log n) because binary search is always required.
quiz.fact: Insertion sort runs in O(n) linear time on an already sorted or nearly sorted array.
why: Each element is compared once with its predecessor and requires no shifts, completing in O(n) time.
No elements need shifting when already in order, so quadratic swaps never occur.
Standard insertion sort compares linearly against neighbors and does not switch to binary search.

quiz.q: What is the primary trade-off of merge sort compared to in-place sorts?
options: It requires O(n) auxiliary space to merge subarrays together.
It slows down to quadratic O(n²) time on reversed arrays.
It cannot guarantee stable ordering for elements with equal keys.
quiz.fact: Merge sort is stable but requires O(n) auxiliary space for merging.
why: Merging two sorted subarrays requires a temporary buffer of size n, costing linear extra space.
Merge sort always runs in O(n log n) time, even when the input array is reversed.
Merge sort preserves the relative order of equal elements, so it is a stable sorting algorithm.

quiz.q: Why does selection sort run in O(n²) time even on a sorted array?
options: It must scan the entire unsorted suffix to find each minimum.
It splits the array into two halves at every recursive step.
It shifts all preceding elements to the right for every item.
quiz.fact: Selection sort repeatedly selects the minimum element from the unsorted suffix and runs in O(n²) time.
why: Selection sort cannot know an element is the minimum without comparing it against every item in the suffix.
Selection sort uses iterative nested loops, not recursive divide-and-conquer splits.
Insertion sort shifts elements rightward, whereas selection sort performs direct swaps into place.
